extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent practitioners, and students of English patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what counts as a patentable invention and the formal/ substantive requirements of patents under English law (statute of James / early common-law doctrine). Covers who is an inventor, what subjects are patentable, novelty/usage tests, specification formalities, and conditions that void a grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory patentability under 21 James I (statute of monopolies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sixth section of 21 James enacts that letters patents for the sole working or making of any manner of new manufactures to the true and first inventor are excepted from the general prohibition of monopolies, provided they are not contrary to the law, nor mischievous to the state, by raising prices of commodities at home, or hurt of trade, or generally inconvenient; the term is generally fourteen years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise treats this statute as declaratory of the Crown's common-law power and as the foundational standard: patents must be for a 'new manufacture', to the 'true and first inventor', and not be 'contrary to the law' or 'mischievous' (e.g., causing price rises or hurting trade). Duration is normally 14 years from the first letters patent. Policy observations on the statute are noted but its legal text provides the primary test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification requirement (particular description and enrolment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A condition was introduced that the inventor must, by an instrument under his hand and seal, particularly describe and ascertain the nature of his invention and in what manner it was to be performed, and cause the same to be enrolled in Chancery within a certain time (generally one month); otherwise the letters patent should utterly cease and become void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification is the substantial part of the monopoly. The description 'must be very correct' — even a slight inadvertent omission can invalidate the patent. The requirement ensures the public receives an equivalent for the limited monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who qualifies as the 'true and first inventor'
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may be (I) a discoverer of a new thing; (II) a publisher of an invention; or (III) an introducer of a foreign invention. The law adjudges the 'true and first inventor' to the person who first communicates/publishes the invention to the public by patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple persons independently discover the same thing, the one who first obtains/publishes by patent is the inventor entitled to the grant. A person who learned the principle from a scientific work, or who was informed of the secret in England by another, is not the inventor. Bringing a foreignly-known invention into England and publishing it can qualify as inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted subjects — what counts as a 'new manufacture'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'new manufacture' has received an extended meaning and may include: (I) a substance or thing made; (II) a machine or instrument; (III) an improvement or addition; (IV) a combination or arrangement of things already known; (V) a principle, method, or process carried into practice by tangible means; (VI) a chemical discovery; (VII) a foreign invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification assists in drafting concise and clear specifications. Although broadly construed, not every discovered thing qualifies: the listed categories indicate the principal kinds courts have treated as within the statute's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary qualities/test for patentable manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Every manufacture within the statute must at least be: 1) New; 2) Not used before (neither by others nor by the inventor); 3) Vendible; 4) Useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition the means must be adapted to the intended end (practical operability). These four are the core TEST by which fitness for patent protection is ascertained; incidental properties are explored when treating specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (what destroys novelty / permitted forms of learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject must be new in the common acceptation and must not be copied from a scientific work; if the subject has been published (even unremarked) it is not new. If two grants have substantially the same object both may be valid only if the modes of attaining the effect are essentially different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty can be lost by prior publication anywhere in the world (though learning the invention abroad does not necessarily defeat patentability). Examples: parts taken from published works (Emerson) defeated novelty; application of a known principle without particularized instrument may be void. Cases (Arkwright, Dolland) illustrate how courts analyze novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use / public use and secrecy rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is void if the subject has been used before: by others, or by the inventor himself prior to obtaining the grant. Knowledge without publication (mere private knowledge) is not necessarily 'use', but if the secret was known to a few and one of them actually used it, a later patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tennant's patent invalid because a bleacher had used the method for years; an inventor's own sale prior to sealing (British imperial verdigris) voided the patent. Whether experimental trials constitute 'use' was unsettled in the treatise. Practical implication: avoid commercial use or sales before sealing; secrecy known to third parties can destroy validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-publisher rule (priority by disclosure/publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two persons separately discover the same thing, the one who first communicates it to the public and/or secures a patent (the publisher) will be adjudged the 'true and first inventor' entitled to the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule encourages early disclosure; a discoverer who does not wish another to obtain a grant should make the discovery public or secure a patent before disclosure. The Dolland and Forsyth v. Reviere examples confirm this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal parts of the letters patent and obligations on grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent contain recitals of the petition, a grant that the grantee and their assigns may make, use, and vend the invention for the time expressed (generally 14 years), commands that others shall not imitate without licence, and directions to officers not to molest the patentee. Certain regulations mentioned in the patent, if not observed, render it void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are either open (litterae patentes) or close (litterae clausae). Grants are public records and must generally be scrutinized in offices and pass by bill to prevent surreptitious grants. The specification clause and other provisos are essential; non-observance of prescribed conditions can invalidate the grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions and grounds that render a patent void
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be declared void if the grant is contrary to the statute of monopolies, leads to use of an invention protected by a prior patent, or if the patentee has transferred or divided it into shares or declared any trust of it to or for any number of persons exceeding five, or those five have acted as a corporate body, or in any way contrary to an act of Parliament recited in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In construing such provisos, executors/administrators are collectively treated as the single person represented. The treatise gives repeated warnings that non-observance of conditions (e.g., specification enrolment, forbidden transfers) will render the entire grant void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rule favoring the grantee
rubrics_metrics.description: The letters patent shall be construed and adjudged in the most favourable and beneficial sense for the best advantage of the grantee, notwithstanding any defective and uncertain description of the nature and quality of the invention, and of its materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule of construction mitigates the consequences of imperfect descriptions in some cases, but does not excuse failures of the specification condition; substantive defects can nevertheless invalidate the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of offices / procedural safeguard against surreptitious grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous offices are established to prevent surreptitious grants: proceedings are inspected by the King's law officers and grants generally must pass by bill so the great seal is not affixed without caution and due consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural framework is part of the patent system's safeguards and affects how a patent is obtained and how its validity may later be assessed; practitioners should follow the prescribed channels to avoid procedural invalidity.
